I was prepared to be. I hadn't encountered the concept before, and expected it to be just another bit of stealth authoritarianism - just another attempt to sell the idea that we'll be made "free" by taking power away from the self-serving scumbags who buy it under current systems and putting it in the hands of "collectives" or "committees" or "associations" or what-have-you, which is to say, putting it in the hands of whichever self-serving scumbags claw their way to the top of those overtly political structures.

I was pleasantly surprised to see that that's not what it is at all. And entirely unsurprised then to see the author include among their critics and opponents "the anarchist movement."

In fact, this controversy is very interesting as it lucidly and concisely expresses the difference between, on the one hand, the defeated world of ideology and all kinds of “-isms”, of closed self-referential systems, gasping to catch up with the new reality, and, on the other hand, the living and outward-looking world of action that strives here and now to disengage from the dominant relations and to self-institute.

The anarchist movement is definitely not what you might encounter in some sections of the USA, especially the west coast. Even more so it is not what it is represented as on the internet and -to the ultimate- what occurs on reddit. Over there I manage a subreddit called r/worldanarchism. It's basically a news and propaganda site that presents the real world of anarchism as a practical movement that exists outside of the internet and which has greater concerns than childish crusades for political correctness. So..."yes Virginia there is an anarchist movement".

I suspect you are something of an individualist and that the mention of some collective form of organization sets off alarm bells for you. My response to that is that the huge number of experiments in self-management afoot in the world today fully recognize the need to adjust any collective decisions with individual needs and freedom. Deal making if you will. Compromise. It's a work in progress, but it is far easier when organizations are concerned with practical questions and not with ideology. Human life is such that 99.99999999 % of us have to adjust our lives and wants to the lives and wants of others. It comes close to being a definition of 'being human'. The difficulty of adjusting the individual to the group and the group to the individual is an ancient one and not open to any ideological solution. Merely practice.

The article in question is to some degree an argument against the various 'leftisms', including those anarchists who have vague romantic goals and ho dislike anything other than loud (and ineffective) militance. There have always been such people amongst the anarchists, those with an abstract idea rather than a plan. At all times, however, they have been balanced by those who have a keener grasp of both morality and daily life.

My response to that is that the huge number of experiments in self-management afoot in the world today fully recognize the need to adjust any collective decisions with individual needs and freedom.

There are no "collective decisions." There are only individual decisions followed by jockeying for position as those so inclined attempt to further one or another justification for seeing their individual decisions imposed upon everyone else. One of the most common of those justifications is to pretend that majority, or even merely plurality, makes ones individual decision a "collective" decision, when it in fact does not and can not. It simply means that those who wish to impose their decision on others sufficiently outnumber those upon whom the decision will be imposed in order to successfully bring about the imposition. Just like that, we've jumped all the way back to "might makes right." Liberty is already dead and we're immediately back to some being forced to submit to the authority of others.

Human life is such that 99.99999999 % of us have to adjust our lives and wants to the lives and wants of others.

Yes - human life is indeed such that the vast majority of us have to adjust our lives and wants to the lives and wants of others. And left to our own devices, we will do exactly that.

The problem is that there are many who are not content to merely adjust their lives and wants to the lives and wants of others. They wish to bypass any need to do so by instead compelling those others to make the adjustments. They'll make a lot of noise about collective this and society that, but that's what it really comes down to - there's a need for some adjustment and they want that adjustment to be made by others in order to accommodate their own lives and wants, and they're just pointing at the purported wants of the purported collective in order to lend credence to their wholly individual desire to avoid having to adjust their lives and wants to others by compelling those others to do the adjusting.

The difficulty of adjusting the individual to the group and the group to the individual is an ancient one and not open to any ideological solution.

This is true. It's not open to any ideological solution (or any other solution, for that matter), since it's a fundamentally flawed concept. If true "anarchism" ever comes to be, it indeed won't be based on some "ideological solution." It will be because enough of humanity has become sufficiently enlightened to stop pretending that individual sovereignty can be rightly denied. Until that time, all we're going to have is different arrangements of those who successfully deny the sovereignty of others and those whose sovereignty is denied - of the rulers and the ruled.

The article in question is to some degree an argument against the various 'leftisms', including those anarchists who have vague romantic goals and ho dislike anything other than loud (and ineffective) militance.
